title: Telluride Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Telluride wells have a 210-foot median depth; finished well costs model at $19,600-$33,000 in fractured mountain bedrock.
h1: Telluride, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Well records within 5 miles of Telluride show a mountain-bedrock setting where drilling results can vary substantially from one lot to the next. Of 673 wells in Colorado DWR permit records, 242 are recorded as constructed, 289 report total depth, and 118 report pump yield.

The useful starting point for a buyer is not a single promised number. It is the local range: the median well is 210 feet deep, the middle half runs from 96 to 445 feet, and reported yields have a median of 12.5 gallons per minute. Those figures help frame bids and due diligence, but they do not guarantee what a new hole will find.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Telluride?
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Telluride is 210 feet. Half of the wells with depth records fall between 96 and 445 feet, while the 90th percentile reaches 650 feet and the deepest record is 1,190 feet.

The depth mix shows why a driller should price the job as a range rather than assume the median: 26% are under 100 feet, 35% are 100-300 feet, 26% are 300-600 feet, and 13% exceed 600 feet. Most permits name an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 632 wells in that category. Granite and gneiss can fracture differently over short distances, so nearby depth records are useful but not a guarantee for your parcel.

sections.heading: Telluride well yields: what can a home expect?
sections.html:
Among 118 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 12.5 gallons per minute and the middle half spans 5.0 to 50.0 gallons per minute. The distribution is stronger than many buyers assume: 47% report more than 15 gallons per minute, 40% report 5-15 gallons per minute, 12% report 1-5 gallons per minute, and 1% report under 1 gallon per minute.

A yield test is still essential. A high-producing neighboring well does not prove the same fracture crosses your lot, and a low-yield well may need storage and careful demand management. Ask for the well construction report, pump test information, and the intended household use before relying on a number in a listing.

sections.heading: Is the water table dropping near Telluride?
sections.html:
Only 25 records report a static water level, so the water-level sample is limited. In those records, the median depth to water is 38 feet, with the middle half between 18 and 74 feet below the surface.

The decade comparison does show a change in the available measurements: the median was 38 feet below surface in the 2010s and 56 feet in the 2020s. That is a deeper measured water level in the later group, but the small number of records and differing well locations mean it should not be treated as proof of a basin-wide decline. Have a qualified professional check the specific well's static level, pumping history, and seasonal behavior.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Telluride, and when?
sections.html:
Permit activity is spread across several decades, with the largest recorded period in the 1990s at 229 permits. The records show 150 permits from the 2000s, 74 from the 2010s, and 29 from the 2020s; the newest permit year is 2025. Earlier records include 9 permits from the 1970s and 48 from the 1980s.

The most active drillers in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), associated with 98 wells; Bill Kissner Drilling Inc, associated with 92; and Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation, associated with 41. These names help when tracing local construction patterns around Telluride, Mountain Village, and Ophir, but a permit record is not a performance warranty. Confirm current licensing, references, and the exact scope of any bid.

sections.heading: What does a new well cost in Telluride?
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss, at roughly $65-$100 per drilled foot. At the 210-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $13,600-$21,000.

A finished system costs more than drilling. With pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical included, the modeled total at the median depth is about $19,600-$33,000. A lot requiring a 445-foot hole or deeper can exceed that range, while a shallow hole may cost less. Get the bid in writing and ask what happens if the hole is dry, the yield is low, casing or grout requirements change, or access is difficult.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building on a Telluride lot
sections.html:
Mining history is a major part of local due diligence. Within about 10 miles, the map shows 4,417 historic mine features, 19 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 8 PFAS sampling or contamination sites. These mapped features do not automatically mean a property is contaminated, but they justify testing the well water and reviewing the site's proximity to mines, drainage pathways, and cleanup areas.

Also check for low yield, dry-hole risk, water-quality treatment, and the separation between the well, septic system, and building area. Confirm that the parcel can support a permitted septic design, access for a large drilling rig, utility trenching, and the intended home location. Colorado DWR permit records and neighboring well reports are valuable starting points, not substitutes for site-specific investigations.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Telluride, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Telluride is 210 feet. The middle half runs from 96 to 445 feet, but the records range as deep as 1,190 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss make depth variable, so nearby permits can guide expectations without predicting the exact depth on a new lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Telluride?
faq.a: The local model uses $65-$100 per foot in fractured mountain bedrock. At the 210-foot median depth, drilling alone is modeled at about $13,600-$21,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $19,600-$33,000. Access, depth, and low-yield complications can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce near Telluride?
faq.a: Among 118 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 12.5 gallons per minute. The middle half reports 5.0-50.0 gallons per minute. Still, 12% produce 1-5 gallons per minute and 1% report under 1 gallon per minute. Require a yield test and plan storage around the actual result.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Telluride?
faq.a: Permit records do not establish that a particular well is safe to drink. The area has 8 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 4,417 historic mine features, and 19 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Test the specific well for relevant contaminants, and review nearby mining and cleanup history before buying.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Telluride?
faq.a: The limited static-water sample has a median depth of 38 feet, with a middle half from 18 to 74 feet. The median measured depth was 38 feet below surface in the 2010s and 56 feet in the 2020s. Only 25 records report static levels, so this suggests a later deeper measurement but does not prove a broad regional decline.
